title: The Sermon on the Mount
subtitle: Matthew 5–7 in 14 days
tagline: The kingdom of heaven, turned right side up.
about: Over two weeks you will read Jesus' most famous teaching, a few verses at a time: the Beatitudes, salt and light, the six 'but I say unto you' contrasts, the Lord's Prayer, and the call to build on the rock. You will come away seeing how Jesus goes beyond outward rule-keeping to the heart, and what life in God's kingdom looks like day to day.

days.title: Blessed Are the Poor
days.focus: Jesus sits down on a mountain and begins with a series of 'blessed are' statements. Notice who he calls blessed: people the world would rarely envy. Notice too the promise attached to each one.
days.context: Teachers in Jesus' day normally sat to teach. Many readers have noticed that Matthew's mountain setting echoes Moses receiving the law at Sinai.

word.why: Each beatitude opens with this word. It describes not a passing mood but a condition of being favored by God; Jesus announces God's favor resting on the poor in spirit, the mourning, the meek, and the hungry.

questions.q: Which group does Jesus say will 'inherit the earth'?
What do you think it means to be 'poor in spirit,' and why might it come first?
Which of these four beatitudes describes something you find hardest to want?

checkIn.q: Where did Jesus go to teach the crowds?
What is promised to those who hunger and thirst after righteousness?

days.title: Mercy, Purity, Peace
days.focus: The beatitudes continue with mercy, a pure heart, peacemaking, and persecution. Notice that the final beatitude shifts from 'they' to 'ye,' speaking straight to the listeners.
days.context: Jesus links his followers with the prophets of Israel, many of whom were rejected or mistreated by their own people.

word.why: This word appears only here in the New Testament. It describes not just peaceful people but those who actively make peace, and Jesus says they will be 'called the children of God' because they resemble their Father.

questions.q: What is promised to the merciful?
Why would peacemakers, of all people, be called 'the children of God'?
Is there a conflict around you where you have been a bystander rather than a peacemaker?

checkIn.q: Who does Jesus say shall see God?
Who, according to verse 12, was persecuted before?

days.title: Salt and Light
days.focus: Jesus uses two everyday images to describe his followers' role in the world. Notice that he says 'Ye are,' not 'try to become.' Notice also who receives the glory when good works are seen.
days.context: Salt preserved and flavored food; the salt of the region often contained impurities and could lose its saltiness. A 'bushel' was a basket used for measuring grain.

word.why: Salt was valuable because it made a difference to whatever it touched. Jesus' warning about salt that has 'lost his savour' (v. 13) suggests that disciples who blend in completely have lost what made them useful.

questions.q: What does Jesus say happens to salt that has lost its savour?
Jesus wants good works seen, yet he wants the Father glorified. How is that different from showing off?
In which setting of your week do you find it hardest to be salt or light?

checkIn.q: Where does Jesus say people do not put a lit candle?
What kind of place 'cannot be hid'?
options: A city set on a hill

days.title: Not to Destroy, but Fulfil
days.focus: Jesus explains how he relates to the Law and the Prophets. Watch for the surprising claim that his followers' righteousness must exceed that of the scribes and Pharisees, who were known for careful obedience.
days.context: A 'jot' is the smallest letter of the Hebrew alphabet (yod), and a 'tittle' is a tiny stroke on a letter. The scribes and Pharisees were widely respected for their attention to the law.

word.meaning: to fulfil, to fill up, to complete
word.why: Jesus did not come to tear down the Law and the Prophets but to 'fulfil' them, bringing them to their intended fullness. Christians explain the details in different ways, but the verses that follow show Jesus going to the heart behind each command.

questions.q: What does Jesus say will not pass from the law 'till all be fulfilled'?
What might a righteousness that 'exceeds' the Pharisees' look like, given how careful they were?
Do you tend to treat God's commands more as a checklist or as a window into his heart?

checkIn.q: What did Jesus say he came to do with the law and the prophets?
Whose righteousness must his followers' righteousness exceed?

days.title: Anger and Reconciliation
days.focus: This is the first of six 'Ye have heard... But I say unto you' contrasts. Jesus traces murder back to anger and contempt, and makes reconciliation more urgent than worship.
days.context: 'Raca' was an Aramaic insult meaning something like 'empty-head.' 'The council' was the Sanhedrin, the Jewish high court, and 'hell fire' translates Gehenna, a valley outside Jerusalem that became a picture of judgment.

word.why: This verb appears only here in the New Testament. Jesus tells a worshipper to leave the gift at the altar and 'first be reconciled to thy brother' (v. 24); the responsibility falls on the one who knows his brother 'hath ought against thee.'

questions.q: What should a person do if they remember at the altar that someone has something against them?
Why does Jesus treat anger and insults as seriously as he does?
Is there a relationship in your life where reconciliation feels overdue?

checkIn.q: Which commandment does Jesus begin with in this passage?
What should you do with your gift if you remember a brother has something against you?
options: Leave it before the altar and go be reconciled
Give it to the poor instead

days.title: Faithful Hearts, Honest Words
days.focus: Jesus addresses lust, divorce, and oaths. In each case he moves past the minimum requirement to the heart: faithfulness in desire, in marriage, and in speech.
days.context: Jewish teachers of the time debated the grounds for divorce, some allowing it for minor reasons, and Jesus' words entered that debate. People sometimes swore by lesser things than God's name to leave themselves a way out of a promise.

word.meaning: to swear, to take an oath
word.why: Jesus says 'Swear not at all' (v. 34) and calls for plain 'Yea, yea; Nay, nay.' The aim is speech so trustworthy it needs no oath; Christians differ on whether this rules out every formal oath, such as one taken in court.

questions.q: What three topics does Jesus address in these verses?
What does the vivid language about plucking out an eye (v. 29) suggest about how seriously Jesus takes sin, and how literally should it be read?
In what situations are you tempted to shade the truth or add extra words to be believed?

checkIn.q: Instead of swearing oaths, what does Jesus say your communication should be?
Which of these does Jesus name as something not to swear by?

days.title: Love Your Enemies
days.focus: Jesus addresses retaliation and love for enemies. Notice the reason he gives: the Father himself sends sun and rain on the evil and the good.
days.context: 'An eye for an eye' was given in the law to limit punishment in the courts, not to license personal revenge. Roman soldiers could legally press civilians into carrying their gear for a mile, which lies behind verse 41.

word.why: 'Be ye therefore perfect' (v. 48) closes this section. In context the word points to being complete in love the way the Father is, a love that does not stop at friends and family.

questions.q: What reason does Jesus give in verse 45 for loving enemies?
How does 'perfect' in verse 48 relate to the examples in verses 43–47?
Who is the hardest person for you to pray for right now?

checkIn.q: If someone compels you to go a mile, what does Jesus say to do?
On whom does the Father make his sun rise?
options: On the evil and on the good

days.title: Seen by the Father
days.focus: Jesus turns to giving and prayer, warning against doing them to be seen. Notice the repeated phrase 'thy Father which seeth in secret' and the promise attached to it.
days.context: Giving to the poor and praying were normal, honored parts of Jewish devotion; Jesus' concern is not public faith but performing for an audience. 'Vain repetitions' refers to piling up words as if to wear God down.

word.why: The word first meant an actor playing a part behind a mask. Jesus uses it for people whose religious acts are a performance for human applause; 'they have their reward' (v. 2), and the applause is all they get.

questions.q: What does Jesus say the hypocrites already have?
If the Father knows what we need before we ask (v. 8), why pray at all?
Whose approval do you most want when you do something good?

checkIn.q: Where does Jesus tell his followers to pray?
options: In their closet, with the door shut

checkIn.q: What should your left hand not know?

days.title: After This Manner Pray
days.focus: Jesus gives a model prayer. Notice the order: God's name, kingdom, and will come first, then daily bread, forgiveness, and protection. Notice also the one line Jesus comments on afterward.
days.context: The closing line in the KJV, 'For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever,' does not appear in the earliest manuscripts and was likely added in early church worship; many modern Bibles place it in a footnote.

word.why: 'Forgive us our debts' (v. 12) pictures sin as something owed. Jesus then explains that receiving forgiveness and extending it belong together (vv. 14–15).

questions.q: Which line of the prayer does Jesus return to and explain in verses 14–15?
Why do you think the prayer begins with God's name and kingdom before our own needs?
Which line of this prayer do you find hardest to pray sincerely?

checkIn.q: What does the prayer ask God to give 'this day'?
According to verse 15, what happens if we do not forgive others?
options: Our Father will not forgive our trespasses

days.title: Where Your Treasure Is
days.focus: Jesus finishes his teaching on fasting, then turns to money and possessions. Watch the connection between where treasure is kept, what the eye fixes on, and which master a person serves.
days.context: Wealth was often stored as fine cloth, grain, or coins, all vulnerable to moths, corrosion, and thieves who could dig through mud-brick walls. 'Mammon' is an Aramaic word for wealth or possessions.

word.why: The word can mean both the treasure and the place it is stored. Jesus' point in verse 21 is that the heart follows the treasure, so where we store what we value shapes what we love.

questions.q: What three things destroy or take away treasure on earth?
What is the connection between 'where your treasure is' and 'there will your heart be also'?
If someone looked at your calendar and spending, what would they conclude you treasure?

checkIn.q: What does Jesus say cannot both be served?
What does Jesus say to do when you fast?
options: Anoint your head and wash your face

days.title: Consider the Lilies
days.focus: Jesus points to birds and wildflowers to address worry about food and clothing. Notice the 'Therefore' that links this to the verses on two masters, and the command to seek first the kingdom.
days.context: 'Take no thought' in 1611 English meant 'do not be anxious,' not 'do not plan.' Dried grasses and wildflowers were commonly burned as fuel in clay ovens.

word.why: This word appears six times in these ten verses. Jesus does not deny that we need food and clothing; he says 'your heavenly Father knoweth' (v. 32), and he treats anxious striving as something the Father's care makes unnecessary.

questions.q: What two examples from nature does Jesus point to?
How does 'seek ye first the kingdom of God' answer the problem of worry, rather than simply telling us to stop?
What worry has been taking up the most room in your thoughts this week?

checkIn.q: Who, in all his glory, was not dressed like one of the lilies?
What does Jesus say to seek first?
options: The kingdom of God and his righteousness

days.title: Specks and Beams
days.focus: Jesus warns against hypocritical judgment with the comic image of a beam in one's own eye. Notice that he does not forbid helping a brother with his speck; he says what has to come first.
days.context: A 'mote' is a speck of dust or straw, and a 'beam' is a large wooden plank. Dogs and pigs were unclean animals in Jewish thought; verse 6 is a puzzling saying that most interpreters take as a call to discernment, though they apply it in different ways.

word.why: 'Judge not' (v. 1) uses a word that can mean simply to assess or to pass sentence. The passage shows Jesus is not forbidding all moral discernment but the self-righteous condemnation that ignores one's own faults.

questions.q: What does Jesus tell the hypocrite to do first?
How can verses 1–5 and verse 6 both be true: no hypocritical judging, yet real discernment?
Which fault in others irritates you most, and do you share it?

checkIn.q: What is in the eye of the person who is judging?
According to verse 2, how will you be judged?
options: With the same judgment you use on others

days.title: Ask, Seek, Knock
days.focus: Jesus encourages persistent prayer grounded in the Father's goodness, then sums up the Law and the Prophets in the Golden Rule. He finishes with two gates and two ways.
days.context: Other teachers of the era had stated the rule negatively; the rabbi Hillel is remembered for saying, in effect, 'what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor.' Jesus states it positively.

word.why: The KJV's 'strait gate' (v. 13) means a narrow one, not a straight one. The word pictures a tight passage hemmed in on both sides, a way that must be deliberately chosen rather than drifted into.

questions.q: What do the three verbs in verse 7 have in common?
Why does Jesus say the Golden Rule 'is the law and the prophets'?
Is there something you have stopped asking God for? What made you stop?

checkIn.q: If a son asks for bread, what will a good father not give him?
Which gate leads to life?

days.title: Built on the Rock
days.focus: Jesus closes with warnings about false prophets, empty profession, and two builders. Notice that both houses face the same storm, and notice how the crowd responds at the very end.
days.context: In the land of Israel, dry stream beds could flood suddenly during winter rains, sweeping away anything built on loose ground.

word.why: The wise man builds on 'a rock' (v. 24), solid bedrock rather than a loose stone. Jesus identifies that foundation as hearing 'these sayings of mine' and doing them.

questions.q: How does Jesus say false prophets will be recognized?
In verses 21–23, people do impressive things in Jesus' name yet are turned away. What is missing?
Which teaching from these two weeks are you hearing but not yet doing?

checkIn.q: Where did the wise man build his house?
Why were the people astonished at the end?
options: He taught as one having authority

leader.intro: This study meets twice: once after the first week (Matthew 5) and once after the second (Matthew 6–7). Plan 60–75 minutes, with about 10 minutes to settle in, 45 minutes of discussion, and 10–15 minutes of prayer. The Sermon on the Mount is familiar enough that people may assume they already know it; slow down, read key sections aloud, and ask what surprised people. Many of these teachings are uncomfortable, so make room for honest questions instead of rushing to tidy answers.

sessions.title: Blessed, Salt, Light, and More
sessions.opening: Who is someone you would describe as truly 'blessed,' and what makes you say so?
discussion: Read 5:3-12 aloud. Which beatitude surprised you most this week, and why?
What do the people Jesus calls blessed have in common? How does that compare with who our culture calls fortunate?
Jesus says 'Ye are the salt of the earth' and 'Ye are the light of the world.' What is the difference between being told 'you are' and 'try to be'?
How did Jesus 'fulfil' the law, based on the six 'But I say unto you' sayings in 5:21-48?
Jesus links anger to murder and lust to adultery. Why focus on the heart rather than only on actions?
What does loving an enemy look like in practice, based on verses 38–48?
Which teaching from Matthew 5 do you find hardest to take seriously, and why?
sessions.notes: Matthew sets the sermon on a mountain, and many readers see an echo of Moses at Sinai: Jesus speaks with his own authority ('But I say unto you') rather than quoting other teachers. The Beatitudes are announcements of God's favor, not a list of entry requirements, so watch for answers that turn them into a to-do list. Verses 17–20 can raise good questions about how Christians relate to the Old Testament law; thoughtful Christians answer differently, and it is fine to say so and keep reading what Jesus actually does in verses 21–48. The teaching on divorce (vv. 31–32) can be painful for group members; acknowledge that Christians apply these words in different ways and avoid singling anyone out. Likewise, 'turn the other cheek' is sometimes misused to tell victims of abuse to stay in danger; the passage is about refusing personal revenge, not about tolerating harm. Verse 48 ('Be ye therefore perfect') can sound crushing; in context it caps a section on love that reaches even to enemies, modeled on the Father's own generosity.
sessions.prayer: Pray by name for someone you find difficult, as Jesus commands in 5:44, and ask God for mercy and a pure heart.

sessions.title: Secret Devotion and Solid Ground
sessions.opening: What is something you have built or made that has lasted, and what made it last?
discussion: In 6:1-18, Jesus addresses giving, prayer, and fasting. What do these three warnings have in common?
Walk slowly through the Lord's Prayer (6:9-13). What does each line ask for, and what does the order teach us?
Why do you think Jesus singles out forgiveness for extra comment in 6:14-15?
How are 'treasure in heaven' (6:19-24) and freedom from worry (6:25-34) connected?
What is the difference between the judging Jesus forbids in 7:1-5 and the discernment he expects in 7:6 and 7:15-20?
In 7:21-27, what separates the wise builder from the foolish one?
After two weeks in this sermon, what is one thing you want to begin doing, not just hearing?
sessions.notes: Chapter 6 is built around three practices that were normal in Jewish devotion (giving, prayer, fasting); Jesus assumes his followers will do them and is concerned with motive. The Lord's Prayer is the centerpiece; some groups enjoy praying it slowly together, pausing after each line. Note that the KJV's closing doxology in 6:13 is absent from the earliest manuscripts, which is why some Bibles footnote it; this does not change the meaning of the prayer. In 6:25-34, 'take no thought' means 'do not be anxious,' not 'do not plan,' and people who live with anxiety may hear these verses as blame; Jesus' tone here is reassurance about the Father's care. 'Judge not' (7:1) is among the most quoted verses in the Bible and is often used to mean that no one can ever say anything is wrong; the passage itself expects removing the beam and then helping with the speck, and 7:15-20 asks for discernment. Verses 21–23 are sobering; let them be sobering without turning the discussion into speculation about who is or isn't saved. End by noticing that the crowd was astonished at his authority (7:28-29).
sessions.prayer: Pray the Lord's Prayer together slowly, then thank God for the rock that holds when storms come.
